sources.news_title: Millions face treacherous conditions as heat dome expands across central US
sources.text:
Millions face treacherous conditions as heat dome expands across central US
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Add The New York Post on GoogleWASHINGTON (AP) — Dangerously hot weather will expand across much of the central United States this weekend and into next week, pushing temperatures above 100 degrees Fahrenheit (37.8 degrees Celsius) from Dallas to North Dakota with roughly 70 million people facing heat advisories.
A heat dome, where atmospheric conditions trap heat, will create sustained high temperatures and accumulating discomfort.
Overnight low temperatures aren’t expected to come down enough for people to have much chance to recover, allowing heat stress to build as the bad weather lingers, forecasters said. The high humidity will make it feel even worse.
A huge stretch of the country will endure the oppressive midsummer weather. It will stretch from the desert Southwest to the Gulf Coast, reaching up into the Midwest and Great Plains.
Some records around the Denver area may be broken, forecasters said. Temperatures are expected to be 10 F to 15 F (5.6 to 8.3 C) above what’s normal.
“It looks like it is going to be pretty much stationary in that position as we go through the week,” said Bob Oravec, meteorologist with the National Weather Service.
Places under a National Weather Service extreme heat warning included western Nebraska, where temperatures Saturday and Sunday were forecast to reach 108 F (42 C).
At the Museum of the Fur Trade near Chadron, Nebraska, there were fewer visitors than usual for this time of year. Meanwhile, fur hats and pelts in the gift shop weren’t selling so hot.
“I’m sure no one would be willing to wear it on a day like this,” said museum employee Hannah Lovelace. Loose-fitting, period-correct fabric shirts, on the other hand, remained popular sellers among folks headed to historical frontier re-enactments called rendezvous, she said.
The region’s heat was forecast to continue through the week, with temperatures topping 100 F (37 C) even in normally moderate areas of Montana and Wyoming.
There might be some relief in the central United States toward next weekend, but even that might be temporary, said Oravec.
Some areas will be spared. The Mid-Atlantic and Northeast should avoid the extreme heat, as will much of the Pacific Northwest.
This is the latest miserable stretch of weather during a summer that has already had a lot of it.
The eastern United States endured an unbearably hot early July that forced communities to cancel Independence Day celebrations and disrupted the country’s 250th anniversary.
Another heat wave in mid-July hit the Southwest and Great Plains. It’s not just the United States. A heat wave in June devastated Europe; France recorded at least 5,700 more deaths than usual during this period.

Fans at the Indianapolis Motor Speedway for the Brickyard 400 on Sunday will be offered water refill stations and places to get cool.
Packed coolers are allowed. In Denver, recreation centers will set aside areas for people to get out of the heat and in front of air conditioning.
This heat dome will be dangerous. Children and the elderly, along with those with medical conditions, are especially at risk of serious conditions including heat stroke.
The basics are important: people should seek out air conditioning or a cooling center and make sure they drink enough water and limit time under the direct sun.
The weather will shift somewhat through the week, with the worst pockets of heat becoming particularly severe across Texas and parts of the Gulf Coast by Wednesday.
It can be difficult to know exactly how climate change contributes to particular events in real time.
But rising carbon dioxide levels from burning fossil fuels makes it more likely that hotter weather becomes more frequent and extreme, according to Andy Pershing, chief program officer at Climate Central, a climate change communications nonprofit.
“We are experiencing exactly what the climate models in the 1990s said we should experience now. That is more frequent, more severe heat waves, bigger temperature anomalies, more humidity, higher overnight temperatures,” Pershing said.
“These are all part and parcel of the climate story.”

Heat dome expands across the central United States, creating dangerous conditions for millions
Heat dome expands across the central United States, creating dangerous conditions for millions
WASHINGTON (AP) — Temperatures hit sweltering highs across much of the central United States on Saturday as forecasters warned that dangerously hot weather from Dallas to North Dakota would push into next week, with roughly 80 million people facing heat advisories.
A heat dome, where atmospheric conditions trap heat, was forecast to create sustained high temperatures and accumulating discomfort. Meanwhile overnight lows were not expected to come down enough for people to have much chance to recover, allowing heat stress to build as the bad weather lingers, forecasters said. With the high humidity, it feels even worse.
The oppressive midsummer weather was forecast to affect a huge stretch of the country, from the desert Southwest to the Gulf Coast and reaching up into the Midwest and Great Plains. Some records around the Denver area could be broken, forecasters said, and temperatures were expected to be 10 F to 15 F (5.6 to 8.3 C) above normal.
“It looks like it is going to be pretty much stationary in that position as we go through the week,” said Bob Oravec, a meteorologist with the National Weather Service.
Hot weather changes plans and makes life harder for those who work outdoors
Places under a National Weather Service extreme heat warning included western Nebraska, where temperatures Saturday and Sunday were forecast to reach 108 F (42 C).
At the Museum of the Fur Trade near Chadron, Nebraska, there were fewer visitors than usual for this time of year. Fur hats and pelts in the gift shop were not selling so hot.
“I’m sure no one would be willing to wear it on a day like this,” museum employee Hannah Lovelace said. Loose-fitting, period-correct fabric shirts, on the other hand, remained popular sellers among folks headed to historical frontier reenactments called rendezvous, she said.
The region’s heat was forecast to continue through the week, with temperatures topping 100 F (37 C) even in normally moderate areas of Montana and Wyoming.
Las Vegas was also expected to see near record-breaking highs. On Saturday, when temperatures reached around 114 F (45 C) in the valley, HVAC repair technician Kristian “Flaco” Santos spent hours outside fixing air conditioning units. His job involves climbing onto homeowners’ roofs or in their attics, where temperatures can be 15 degrees warmer.
“It is brutal,” Santos said, adding that not everyone can work in the heat. “I’m not Superman, but I do, I do take care of myself when I’m in the heat.”
Santos wears long-sleeve shirts and hoodies to protect himself from the sun, drinks lots of water with electrolytes to stay hydrated and takes small breaks to cool down. He encouraged people who work outside to do the same.
“You want to get home to your family safe,” Santos said.
There might be some relief in the central U.S. toward next weekend, but even that might be temporary, Oravec said.
Some areas will be spared. The Mid-Atlantic and Northeast should avoid the extreme heat, as will much of the Pacific Northwest.
This is the latest miserable stretch of weather during a summer that has already had a lot of it. The eastern U.S. endured an unbearably hot early July that forced communities to cancel Independence Day celebrations and disrupted the country’s 250th anniversary. Another heat wave in mid-July hit the Southwest and Great Plains.
It’s not just the United States: A June heat wave devastated Europe, with France recording at least 5,700 more deaths than usual.
On Sunday at the Indianapolis Motor Speedway, fans for the Brickyard 400 will be offered water refill stations and places to get cool, and packed coolers will be allowed. In Denver, recreation centers will set aside areas for people to get out of the heat and in front of air conditioning.
In an already hot year, heat extremes are dangerous
Authorities warned that this heat dome will be dangerous. Children and older adults, along with people with medical conditions, are especially at risk of serious conditions including heat stroke. The basics are important: Seek out air conditioning or a cooling center, and make sure to drink enough water and limit time under the direct sun.
The weather will shift somewhat through the week, with the worst pockets of heat becoming particularly severe across Texas and parts of the Gulf Coast by Wednesday.
It can be difficult to know exactly how climate change contributes to particular events in real time. But rising carbon dioxide levels from burning fossil fuels makes it more likely that hotter weather becomes more frequent and extreme, said Andy Pershing, chief program officer at Climate Central, a climate change communications nonprofit.
“We are experiencing exactly what the climate models in the 1990s said we should experience now. That is more frequent, more severe heat waves, bigger temperature anomalies, more humidity, higher overnight temperatures,” Pershing said. “These are all part and parcel of the climate story.”
The continental U.S. endured the second-hottest first half of the year on record in 2026, according to average temperature tracking by the National Centers for Environmental Information. June itself was the 18th warmest.

sources.news_title: Central U.S. Will Experience ‘Hazardous Heat’ Through Monday—These States Will Be The Hottest
sources.text:
Topline
High heat bearing down on the central U.S. this weekend will continue through Monday, according to the National Weather Service, with roughly 70 million people facing severe heat risks.
Key Facts
“Hazardous heat” is forecast to build "steadily" into the Great Basin and Northern Plains through the weekend, with widespread major heat risks and isolated extreme heat risks in places from the Rockies toward the Mississippi Valley and south to the Gulf Coast, according to the NWS.
The NWS defines major heat risk as temperatures dangerous to those without “proper hydration or adequate cooling,” noting those in living spaces without air conditioners could be exposed to “deadly” temperatures.
The heat risk map for Sunday forecasts major risks in North Dakota, South Dakota, Nebraska, Kansas, Oklahoma, Arkansas, Mississippi, Missouri, Iowa, Minnesota, Wisconsin and Florida—many of which have small pockets of places with extreme heat risk.
High temperatures will generally range from the upper 90s to lower 100s in central and southern states, with isolated areas in the Southwest experiencing temperatures up to 120 degree Fahrenheit, according to the NWS.
What To Watch For
Major heat risks are forecast to dissipate in some parts of the central U.S. by Friday, when high temperatures will grow in the South and Southwest.
Crucial Quote
“High temperatures combined with high humidity can raise heat indices to 105 to 115 degrees, which will pose health risk concerns to anyone without adequate cooling or hydration,” NWS noted. Heat indices measure what temperatures feel like to the human body, not the temperature itself.
Key Background
The seasonal temperature outlook for August, September and October calls for slightly above or above normal temperatures in a majority of the U.S., with much of the central U.S. expected to have equal chances of lower-than-usual or higher-than-usual temperatures. El Niño, a climate pattern that is characterized by warmer-than-average ocean surface temperatures, developed in the tropical Pacific last month and is expected to strengthen, according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. El Niño typically results in a warmer than usual winter in the northern U.S. and an increase in storms in the southern tier of the U.S.

sources.news_title: Midwest And Plains Brace For Hottest Stretch Of Summer As Massive Heat Dome Shifts East - Tampa Free Press
sources.text:
A high-pressure heat dome that has generated record-breaking temperatures across the western portion of the country is moving eastward, bringing the summer’s most intense heat to millions across the Central states and Mississippi Valley through the end of July.
The weather pattern arrives following a multi-day heat wave in the interior West, where Phoenix, Arizona, tentatively tied its all-time record high minimum temperature of 97 degrees Fahrenheit on Friday morning.
Temperatures across the Texas Panhandle are expected to reach or exceed 105 degrees for several consecutive days, while record highs remain possible in northern cities like Billings, Montana, and Bismarck, North Dakota, where forecasts call for peaks near 107 degrees through the weekend.
“The core of the brutal heat will gradually shift out of Montana and the Dakotas through Sunday and head farther south and east as we go into next week,” AccuWeather Senior Meteorologist Joe Lundberg said. “When the intense heat backs off next week, most days will remain in the 90s through next week in that area. Meanwhile, the heat will escalate farther south in Kansas, Oklahoma, Texas and portions of the Mississippi Valley.”
By early next week, major metropolitan areas including Kansas City, St. Louis, and Memphis are projected to hit or surpass 100 degrees over multiple days. High humidity levels will further elevate heat indexes across the region.
“Not only will it be extremely hot, but it will be exceptionally humid as well, particularly over the Mississippi Valley,” Lundberg said. “The combination of the two will drive AccuWeather RealFeel® Temperatures to 110 degrees or higher.”
Temperatures in that range carry elevated risks for heat-related illnesses, including heat cramps, heat exhaustion, and heatstroke for individuals spending extended periods outdoors.
Thunderstorms moving into the region by Tuesday night or Wednesday are expected to offer partial relief, lowering daytime highs into the low-to-mid-90s across affected areas.
Heat index values may still approach 100 degrees during afternoon hours as the high-pressure system pushes back toward the West. Long-range forecasts indicate temperatures will likely remain above historical averages across the Central and Eastern states through mid-August.

sources.news_title: Dangerous Heat Expected Across The State
sources.text:
(Des Moines) The National Weather Service in Des Moines is warning residents across parts of central, south central and southwest Iowa about dangerous heat conditions expected through Monday.
A Heat Advisory is in effect from noon today through noon Sunday, with heat index values near or above 105 degrees expected.
An Extreme Heat Warning will be in effect from noon to 9 p.m. Sunday, when heat index values could reach 112 degrees. An Extreme Heat Watch is also in effect from Sunday evening through Monday evening, with heat index values up to 110 degrees possible.
The National Weather Service says heat-related illnesses increase significantly during periods of extreme heat and high humidity. Residents are encouraged to drink plenty of fluids, stay in air-conditioned rooms, avoid the sun and check on relatives and neighbors.
